b1plus-noun-clause-dik.title: Noun Clauses with -DIk (Knowing/Saying That...)
b1plus-noun-clause-dik.explanation: You already used -DIk to build relative clauses (the book [that] I read). The same participle, now carrying a possessive suffix to mark WHO does the action and a case suffix to mark its role in the sentence, turns a whole clause into a noun: 'Onun geldiğini biliyorum' (I know that he came/is coming) literally means 'I know his coming.' The same pattern extends naturally to the future with -EcEk instead of -DIk: 'Geleceğini biliyorum' (I know that he will come).
b1plus-noun-clause-dik.fact: A -DIk noun clause doesn't have a strict present/past split the way an English 'that'-clause does: geldiğini can mean 'that he came' or 'that he is coming' depending on context, since the participle marks realized fact, not a specific tense.

dialogue.tr: Onun bu işi bitirdiğini biliyor musun?
dialogue.en: Do you know that he finished this job?
Yes, I know, I heard that he worked a lot.

b1plus-noun-clause-ma.title: Noun Clauses with -mA (Wanting Someone to Do)
b1plus-noun-clause-ma.explanation: -DIk clauses report facts. -mA clauses express desires, requests, or actions that aren't (yet) real. istemek always takes -mA: 'Gitmemi istiyor' (He wants me to go) literally means 'he wants my going.' The same -mA nominal is used after asking/allowing/suggesting verbs (rica etmek, izin vermek, teklif etmek) and after postpositions like -DAn (hoşlanmak, korkmak) and -(y)A (başlamak, devam etmek).
b1plus-noun-clause-ma.fact: The choice between -DIk and -mA isn't about tense, it's about reality: -DIk marks something that happened or is a known fact, -mA marks something wanted, possible, or not-yet-real. 'Geldiğini biliyorum' (I know he came, a fact) vs 'Gelmesini istiyorum' (I want him to come, not yet real).

dialogue.en: What do you want from me?

b1plus-past-continuous.title: Past Continuous and Future-in-the-Past
b1plus-past-continuous.pattern: -Iyor + du (was doing); -EcEk + ti (was going to do)
b1plus-past-continuous.explanation: You know -Iyor (present continuous) and -EcEk (future). Add the past copula -DI to either and the whole frame shifts into the past: 'yapıyordum' (I was doing), 'yapacaktım' (I was going to do). A third related pattern, aorist + -DI, means 'used to': 'okurdum' (I used to read) describes a repeated past habit rather than a single moment in progress.
b1plus-past-continuous.fact: -EcEktI often carries the extra flavor of 'but it didn't happen': 'Gelecektim ama gelemedim' (I was going to come but I couldn't) — a broken plan, not just a neutral future-in-the-past.

dialogue.en: What were you doing last night?
I was watching a movie, then I went to sleep early.

b1plus-zorunda.title: Obligation: zorunda and mecbur
b1plus-zorunda.explanation: -mAlI and gerekmek express general obligation or advice. zorunda olmak is stronger: a real, often external constraint. 'Gitmek zorundayım' (I have to go) feels heavier than 'gitmeliyim' (I should go). mecbur olmak/kalmak works the same way, but takes the dative infinitive: 'gitmeye mecburum.'
b1plus-zorunda.fact: 'zorunda kalmak' (rather than 'olmak') specifically frames the obligation as something that happened TO you — a situation forced your hand — while 'zorunda olmak' just states that the constraint exists.

dialogue.en: Why did you get up so early?
I had to catch the flight.

b1plus-diye.title: Reported Speech with diye
b1plus-diye.explanation: Turkish often reports speech and thought by quoting it directly and following with diye ('saying that') plus a reporting verb: 'Yarın geliyorum' diye söyledi (He said, 'I'm coming tomorrow'). diye also introduces reported questions and thoughts: 'Nereye gidiyorsun?' diye sordu (He asked, 'Where are you going?'). This sits alongside the -DIk-clause method (Geldiğini söyledi) as a second, very common way to report speech — and diye can also express a reason or worry: 'Geç kalırım diye koştum' (I ran, thinking I might be late).
b1plus-diye.fact: diye comes from demek (to say) and functions like an invisible quotation mark: unlike English reported speech, it doesn't shift tense or person — the quoted part stays exactly as it was said.

b1plus-indefinites.title: Indefinite Pronouns and Quantifiers
b1plus-indefinites.explanation: her (every) + noun, herkes (everyone), herhangi bir (any/whichever), hiç (not... any/never, used with a negative verb), hiçbir (not a single), hiç kimse (nobody), birkaç (a few), birçok (many), bazı (some). her and hiçbir attach directly before a singular noun; birkaç/birçok/bazı can take a plural noun.
b1plus-indefinites.fact: hiç alone (without bir) means 'at all / ever' and pairs with a negative verb: 'Hiç gitmedim' (I've never been), while hiçbir specifically means 'not a single X': 'Hiçbir şey anlamadım' (I understood nothing at all).

dialogue.tr: Bu konuda hiç fikrin var mı?

b1plus-comparison-extended.title: Extended Comparison: kadar, ne kadar...o kadar
b1plus-comparison-extended.pattern: X kadar Y (as Y as X); ne kadar...o kadar (the more...the more)
b1plus-comparison-extended.explanation: kadar means 'as much as / to the extent of.' 'Senin kadar çalışkanım' (I'm as hardworking as you). Negate with değil: 'Onun kadar hızlı değilim' (I'm not as fast as him). For 'the more X, the more Y,' pair ne kadar with o kadar: 'Ne kadar çok çalışırsan, o kadar çok kazanırsın' (The more you work, the more you earn).
b1plus-comparison-extended.fact: kadar can also attach to a -DIk clause to compare actions, not just nouns: 'Düşündüğüm kadar kolay değildi' (It wasn't as easy as I thought).

dialogue.en: It's not as hard as you think.

b1plus-esi-gelmek.title: Feeling Like Doing: -esi gelmek
b1plus-esi-gelmek.explanation: To say you suddenly feel like doing something, attach -esi (or -ası after back vowels) to the verb stem, add a possessive suffix, then follow with gelmek: 'Ağlayasım geldi' (I felt like crying), 'Gülesim geliyor' (I feel like laughing). It's a vivid, natural way to describe a sudden impulse, more colorful than plainly saying istiyorum.
b1plus-esi-gelmek.fact: Because gelmek (to come) is the finite verb here, it conjugates for tense normally while -esi+possessive stays fixed: 'içesim geldi' (I felt like drinking, past), 'içesim geliyor' (I feel like drinking, now), 'içesim gelecek' (I'll feel like drinking).

dialogue.en: I don't know, I don't feel like doing anything.

b1plus-causative.title: Causative Voice: -t, -DIr, and Irregular Forms
b1plus-causative.pattern: vowel/l/r-final polysyllabic stem + -t (okutmak); most other stems + -DIr/-tIr (yaptırmak); a closed set of monosyllabic verbs are irregular (pişirmek, korkutmak) or fully suppletive (getirmek, götürmek, göstermek)
b1plus-causative.explanation: The causative voice means 'make/have someone do X.' Polysyllabic vowel-, l-, or r-final stems take -t: oku-t-mak (have someone read), büyü-t-mek (raise/grow something), kızar-t-mak (fry). Most other stems take the productive -DIr/-tIr (4-way harmony + voicing): yap-tır-mak (have made), yaz-dır-mak (have written), kes-tir-mek (have cut). A small closed set of common monosyllabic verbs is irregular and must be learned individually: pişmek→pişirmek (cook), içmek→içirmek (make drink), korkmak→korkutmak (scare), kaçmak→kaçırmak (miss/cause to flee). A few pairs are fully suppletive, unrelated words: gelmek→getirmek (bring), gitmek→götürmek (take/carry), görmek→göstermek (show), öğrenmek→öğretmek (teach).
b1plus-causative.fact: uyumak looks monosyllabic but is historically vowel-final (uyu-), so it follows the REGULAR -t pattern: uyutmak (put to sleep) — don't confuse it with the irregular pişirmek-type list just because it sounds short.
